title: Europe's Rearmament Turned Indian Shells Into a Rs 38,000 Crore Export Story
excerpt: India's defence exports hit a record Rs 38,424 crore in FY2025-26, and Bloomberg's trade-data analysis shows at least $872 million of Indian shells, mortars and explosives shipped to Europe since 2022.
body:
• India's defence exports reached a record Rs 38,424 crore in FY2025-26, up about 62.7% from Rs 23,622 crore the previous year, according to Ministry of Defence figures cited by Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh.
  • A Bloomberg analysis of trade data found Indian firms shipped at least $872 million of artillery shells, mortar rounds, propellants and explosives to Europe since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine — roughly 16 times the $49.2 million of the four pre-war years.
  • India is now the second-largest supplier of that ammunition class to a 13-country Central and Eastern European bloc, behind only South Korea, and the third-largest arms exporter to Europe overall, Singh said, citing the Bloomberg report.
  • The boom is built on basic ammunition, not marquee platforms: no fighter jets or missiles headline it — scale for makers such as Munitions India and Solar Industries does.

Europe's scramble to rebuild its ammunition stocks has quietly rewired one corner of global defence trade. India's defence exports hit a record Rs 38,424 crore (about €3.6 billion) in the financial year 2025-26, and Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh says the country has become the third-largest exporter of arms to Europe — "mainly because of the Rearm Europe initiative," as he put it, citing a Bloomberg report.

"A lot of standard ammunition of different types, artillery shells, and large- and small-calibre ammunition started getting exported to Europe in significant numbers," Singh told reporters in October. The Ministry of Defence figures he cited put FY2025-26 exports at Rs 38,424 crore, a rise of about 62.7% over Rs 23,622 crore in FY2024-25, with Indian defence products now reaching more than 80 countries.

The $872 million ammunition flow

The European leg of that growth is concentrated in the least glamorous part of the catalogue. Bloomberg's analysis of trade data, reported in October, found Indian manufacturers have shipped at least $872 million worth of shells, mortar rounds, propellants and explosives to Europe since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. In the four years before the war, the same flow was worth $49.2 million — an increase of roughly 1,600%.

About three-quarters of the shipments went to 13 Central and Eastern European countries, where India has climbed from 28th place four years ago to become the second-biggest supplier of this ammunition class, behind only South Korea. Romania, Slovenia, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Bulgaria, Croatia and Poland are among the largest customers, according to Swarajya's summary of the Bloomberg data. Beyond ammunition, India's export basket to Europe and elsewhere includes artillery systems, small arms, helmets and bulletproof jackets.

Why Europe is buying

The demand side is policy, not fashion. The European Union's ReArm Europe plan, developed under its Readiness 2030 framework, is designed to mobilise up to €800 billion in additional defence investment, and member states that sent their own shell stocks to Ukraine are refilling magazines faster than Europe's traditional suppliers can expand production. Indian factories — state-owned Munitions India and private players such as Solar Industries among them — offered available capacity in standard calibres.

One sensitivity runs through the trade: some Indian shells have reportedly reached Ukraine via European buyers. Indian officials have said end-user rules place responsibility for onward transfer on the buyer, a position that lets New Delhi sell into Europe's rearmament without formally arming either side of the war — even as the flow undercuts Russia, historically India's own largest arms supplier.

What to watch

Two cautions belong with the headline number. First, the rankings describe ammunition and defence-goods trade, not the major-platform transfers — combat aircraft, warships, missile systems — that SIPRI's arms-transfer rankings measure on a different methodology; India is not suddenly a top-three global arms power. Second, ammunition demand is war-driven: a ceasefire or a European production surge would test how much of this market India keeps. For now, the export line gives Indian defence manufacturing something it has long lacked — volume — and gives investors in listed defence names a concrete order-book story rather than a slogan. A fuller account of the official figures is at IndUS Business Journal.
